newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's PM criticised over graft remarks.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's PM criticised over graft remarks.

text.p: A senior aide to Vietnam's Communist Party chief on Thursday criticised a speech by the country's reformist Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet for failing to outline concrete steps against corruption.

In an unusually frank interview with the Tuoi Tre newspaper, Le Duc Binh, assistant to Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi, was quoted as saying Kiet had failed to present solutions to the problem in a rousing speech to the National Assembly.
"In his speech to the National Assembly Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet used most of the time to talk about the fight against corruption," Binh said.

"I support that determination. However, I think both the Prime Minister's report and the National Assembly resolutions for 1997 show still too much talk but no concrete solutions..." the newspaper quoted him as saying.
State-controlled media quoted Kiet last week as calling, in his speech, for proper recognition of his constitutional rights to punish corrupt officials.
"If it is possible, first...please allow prime ministers to have full power in fighting against corruption," he said.
Kiet, 73, is one of the three most powerful people in Vietnam. He occupies a position in the leadership triumvirate alongside Muoi, 79, and President Le Duc Anh, 75.
But Binh's interview on Thursday echoed statements made earlier by Muoi that immediate action was needed to fight graft, and outlined a number of measures to tackle the problem.

He said government officials should be compelled to declare assets regardless of rank, rumours of corrupt practices should be investigated and business sponsorship for officials' wives or children to travel outside Vietnam prohibited.
He did not elaborate or make clear whether he was referring to specific individuals.
Corruption is endemic in Vietnam. The country was ranked earlier this year by an independent Hong Kong consultancy as one of the three most graft-ridden in Asia.
While the issue is not new, it has come to assume major political proportions in recent months.
Two senior officials at Vietcombank, the country's biggest state-owned commercial bank, have been implicated in a major corruption case involving Ho Chi Minh City firm Tamexco.
Earlier this month National Assembly delegates voted to dismiss chief prosecutor Le Thanh Dao over what a foreign ministry official described as "mistakes and involvement in a business wrongdoing".
Dao is now being investigated over the allegations.
Binh's comments mark an apparent break with a tradition in Vietnam's Communist government of presenting an image of unanimity. Public criticism of leaders is extremely rare.
